title: pprof: CPU and heap profiling, escape analysis (-gcflags=-m)
summary: pprof samples where a program spends CPU time and where it allocates, down to the source line; go build -gcflags=-m explains why a value lives on the heap. Profile a benchmark or a running service, fix the top entry, measure again.

examples.title: A CPU profile finds the quadratic loop nobody suspected

annotations.note: One loop, one append: it reads as linear. slices.Contains scans out on every iteration, so it is O(n²), and nothing on the page looks expensive. This is why guessing fails.
format uses fmt and reflection, the usual suspect in a code review. It doesn't appear in the profile at all.

While profiling is on, the runtime records the running goroutine's stack 100 times per second of CPU time. Overhead is low enough for production, but it is a sample: a 200 ms run gives about 20 stacks.

-top lists functions; -cum sorts by cumulative time (the function plus everything it calls) instead of flat time (the function's own instructions). cum finds the expensive path, flat the instructions burning the time.
The table is real pprof output; only the header (binary path, date, sample count) is cut. Timings differ on every run, which is why this example is checked with "contains".

examples.title: A heap profile names the function and the line that allocate

annotations.note: By default the runtime records one allocation per 512 KiB allocated, on average, and pprof scales the samples up. Rate 1 records every allocation so the numbers are exact and repeatable; it is far too slow for production.
2,000 concatenations, each copying everything so far: about 20 MB allocated to build a 20 KB string. The CSV parsing that looks busier allocates less than 0.1 MB.
A heap profile reports as of the last completed GC, so collect first. go test -memprofile does the same before writing its profile.

alloc_space counts every byte allocated since start; the default, inuse_space, counts only what is still live, which here is almost nothing. Use alloc_* to find churn that keeps the GC busy, inuse_* to find memory that is retained or leaking.
-list takes a regular expression and prints the source of matching functions with per-line totals: the profile points at line 29, not just at render.

examples.title: go build -gcflags=-m: the compiler's heap decisions, one per function

annotations.note: "moved to heap: p": the address is returned, so p must outlive the call. One allocation per NewPoint, which is fine unless NewPoint is in a hot loop.
"&Point{...} does not escape": taking an address costs nothing when the pointer never leaves the function; the struct stays on the stack.
The slice is returned, so its backing array must be on the heap.

"does not escape" is not "never allocates". The size is known only at run time; since Go 1.25 the compiler keeps a small buffer on the stack and falls back to the heap when n doesn't fit (in an AllocsPerRun test on Go 1.27, 32 bytes fit and 33 did not).
Nothing escapes, yet buf is moved to the heap: a 1 MiB variable is too large for a goroutine stack frame.
fmt.Sprint takes ...any, so p.X is converted to an interface and "escapes". The variadic slice itself stays on the stack ("... argument does not escape").
-gcflags=-m applies to the packages named on the command line; -m=2 explains each decision, and -gcflags=all=-m includes every dependency. The example filters out the "can inline" lines.
Positions are file:line:column in esc.go, whose first line is line 12 of this file: esc.go:8:2 is the p := Point{x, y} on line 19 here.

use_cases: A slow benchmark: go test -bench=Name -cpuprofile cpu.out, then go tool pprof -top or -http=:8081 cpu.out
A service using too much CPU or memory: import net/http/pprof on a localhost-only listener and pull a 30-second profile
GC pressure: a heap profile with -sample_index=alloc_space, then -gcflags=-m on the hot package to see why values escape
Goroutine leaks: the goroutine profile, and since Go 1.27 the goroutineleak profile
Profile-guided optimization: commit a representative CPU profile as default.pgo next to main
strengths: Built into the runtime and the go command: no agent, no separate profiler install, unlike Java's async-profiler or JFR setup
Sampling keeps CPU profiling overhead low enough to run in production, unlike Python's instrumenting cProfile
Profiles carry symbols and inlining information, so -list maps samples to source lines, inlined calls included
Escape decisions are printable on demand, where the JVM's escape analysis happens invisibly in the JIT
weaknesses: A profile is a statistical sample: short runs and rare paths can be missing or noisy
Heap profiles show where memory was allocated, not who holds it now; finding a retention path needs reasoning or a heap dump
-gcflags=-m output changes between Go versions, so don't build tooling that parses it
The CPU profile shows on-CPU time; time spent waiting for locks, I/O or the database needs the block, mutex or trace views

pitfalls.title: Optimizing without a profile
pitfalls.detail: The expensive code is often the innocent-looking loop, not the reflection-heavy formatter. Profile a benchmark or production first, fix the top entry, and measure again.

pitfalls.title: Exposing net/http/pprof on the public listener
pitfalls.detail: The blank import registers /debug/pprof/ on http.DefaultServeMux. Serve that mux on 127.0.0.1 only, separately from the application's own mux.
pitfalls.bad: import _ "net/http/pprof" // and the public server uses DefaultServeMux
pitfalls.good: go func() { log.Println(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:6060", nil)) }() // app uses its own mux

pitfalls.title: Reading inuse_space when hunting garbage
pitfalls.detail: The default heap view shows live memory. Short-lived garbage that drives GC cost appears only under alloc_space or alloc_objects.

pitfalls.title: Taking 'does not escape' as 'no allocation'
pitfalls.detail: Variable-size make and very large locals can still use the heap. Confirm with testing.AllocsPerRun or -benchmem.

pitfalls.title: Profiling with the race detector or coverage on
pitfalls.detail: -race and -cover change the code being measured. Profile a normal build.

quiz.q: In pprof -top, main.handle has flat 0 and cum 95%. What does that mean?
options: It does almost no work itself; functions it calls account for 95% of the samples
quiz.why: flat counts samples where the function was executing its own code; cum counts samples where it was anywhere on the stack.

quiz.q: You want the code that creates the most short-lived garbage. Which heap view?
quiz.why: inuse_* shows what is still live; garbage has already been collected and appears only in the alloc_* totals.

quiz.q: -gcflags=-m prints 'make([]byte, n) does not escape'. Can that line still allocate on the heap?
options: Yes: with a size known only at run time, a large n falls back to the heap
quiz.why: 'Does not escape' means the slice doesn't outlive the function. Since Go 1.25 a small stack buffer covers small sizes; larger ones are heap allocated. Large fixed-size locals are moved to the heap too.

quiz.q: How should a production service expose pprof?
options: Register net/http/pprof on the public mux behind a feature flag
Serve http.DefaultServeMux with the pprof handlers on a localhost-only listener
Write a CPU profile to disk continuously
quiz.why: Profiles reveal internals and a CPU profile request costs CPU for its duration; keep the endpoint off the public listener and reach it through SSH or kubectl port-forward.

further_reading.title: A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector: optimization guide

body:
## Concept

pprof is Go's built-in profiler, in three parts: the runtime collects samples,
`runtime/pprof`, `net/http/pprof` and `go test` write them as profile files, and
`go tool pprof` reads and presents them. The profiles you will use most:

- **cpu**: where on-CPU time goes, sampled 100 times per second.
- **heap**: allocations by call stack, viewable as `inuse_space`/`inuse_objects`
  (live now) or `alloc_space`/`alloc_objects` (since start).
- **goroutine**, **block**, **mutex**: what goroutines are doing and where they wait.
  Go 1.27 adds **goroutineleak**, goroutines blocked on something no runnable
  goroutine can ever reach.

The workflow is a loop: reproduce the load (a benchmark, or a real service under
traffic), collect a profile, read the top entries, change one thing, measure again.
A benchmark run from the scratch module behind the first example, on the author's
machine:

```
$ go test -bench=Dedupe -benchmem -cpuprofile cpu.out
BenchmarkDedupe-32   625   1860894 ns/op   60032 B/op   14 allocs/op
$ go tool pprof -list Dedupe cpu.out
ROUTINE ======================== example.com/report.Dedupe in .../report.go
         0      1.11s (flat, cum) 97.37% of Total
         .          .      5:func Dedupe(ids []int) []int {
         .          .      6:	var out []int
         .          .      7:	for _, id := range ids {
         .      1.11s      8:		if !slices.Contains(out, id) {
         .          .      9:			out = append(out, id)
```

Replacing the scan with a `map[int]struct{}` set brought it to 87524 ns/op, 21 times
faster, at 207802 B/op and 31 allocs/op: CPU and memory profiles can pull in
opposite directions, so measure both. `go tool pprof -http=:8081 cpu.out` opens the
same data in a browser, with a flame graph as the default view since Go 1.26.

When a heap profile points at a line, `go build -gcflags=-m` tells you why the value
there lives on the heap: it escapes (returned, stored, captured, converted to an
interface) or is too large for the stack.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: JFR and async-profiler give similar sampled CPU and allocation views; in
  Go there is nothing to attach, the profiler is in every binary. The JVM's escape
  analysis is a JIT detail you can't easily see; Go prints its decisions at compile
  time.
- **Python**: `cProfile` instruments every call and distorts timings; pprof samples,
  like py-spy. Python has no stack allocation to reason about at all.
- **JS/Node**: Chrome DevTools and `node --cpu-prof` are sampling CPU profilers too.
  V8 heap snapshots show the object graph; Go's heap profile shows allocation sites
  instead, which is better for finding churn and worse for finding who retains what.
- **C/C++**: `perf` works on Go binaries, but pprof understands goroutines, inlined
  frames and Go symbol names without extra setup. There is no `new` vs stack choice:
  escape analysis makes it for you.

## How it works

For CPU profiles the runtime interrupts threads running Go code at 100 Hz and
records the current goroutine's stack; pprof merges identical stacks and counts
them. **flat** is the samples where a function was at the top of the stack, **cum**
those where it appeared anywhere. Inlined calls are kept as separate frames marked
`(inline)`, which is why `slices.Index` shows up with all the flat time although it
was compiled into `dedupe`.

For heap profiles, `mallocgc` records a stack for one allocation per
`runtime.MemProfileRate` bytes (512 KiB by default) and pprof scales the counts
back up. Profiles are only updated at the end of a GC cycle, so a profile can lag
the program by up to two cycles; collecting first gives a current one.

To profile a service, the blank import registers handlers on
`http.DefaultServeMux`. If the application serves its own mux, as StackLab's does,
serve the default mux on a separate localhost listener:

```go
import _ "net/http/pprof"

go func() { log.Println(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:6060", nil)) }()
```

```
go tool pprof http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30
go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_space http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/heap
```

## Design notes

Keep the profile loop cheap and routine. Benchmarks with `b.Loop` and `-benchmem`
make the CPU and allocation cost of hot functions visible in review; `pprof` explains
the numbers; `-gcflags=-m` explains the allocations. Fix the top entry, not the one
you expected, and keep the benchmark so the fix stays fixed.

A CPU profile from production is also a build input. Saved as `default.pgo` in the
main package's directory, it is picked up by `go build` (the default `-pgo=auto`),
which then inlines and devirtualizes more aggressively along the hot paths; the
Go 1.22 notes report 2 to 14% gains for most programs. The profile must come from
representative load, and it is worth refreshing when the code changes a lot.

expected.cpu-profile:
30000 unique lessons

main.dedupe (inline)
slices.Index[go.shape.[]int,go.shape.int] (inline)
expected.heap-profile:
flat 20.11MB  cum 20.11MB  main.render
flat 0.06MB   cum 0.09MB   main.parse
flat 0.01MB   cum 20.21MB  main.main
line 29: 20.11MB  out += "lesson " + strconv.Itoa(id) + "\n"
expected.escape-analysis:
$ go build -gcflags=-m .
./esc.go:8:2: moved to heap: p
./esc.go:13:7: &Point{...} does not escape
./esc.go:17:38: make([]byte, n) escapes to heap
./esc.go:20:13: make([]byte, n) does not escape
./esc.go:25:6: moved to heap: buf
./esc.go:29:47: ... argument does not escape
